claims.text: Restricting precursor mobility governs the successful low-temperature formation of homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Single-phase alloy nanoparticles can form even when the different noble-metal precursors are reduced sequentially.
Restricted mobility causes stochastic, random incorporation of atoms into the nanoparticles.
The starting material is a uniformly mixed collection of noble-metal single-source precursors.
The proposed starting materials can be either bimetallic or five-element mixtures.
A faster reduction rate or a mobility-limiting additive can inhibit atomic or precursor mobility.
The relevant synthesis regime is low-temperature reduction.
Controlled cooling and an inert atmosphere are required conditions for the proposed low-temperature comparison.
Rapid stochastic incorporation enhances homogeneous atomic mixing.
Homogeneous atomic mixing produces attendant lattice strain.
Limiting the mobility of reduced atoms suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
Mobility inhibition favors stochastic formation of a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The mobility-inhibition effect becomes more pronounced as the number of distinct elements increases.
Mobility-restricted five-element noble-metal systems should form homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles more frequently than otherwise identical higher-mobility controls.
Binary noble-metal systems may require cooperative reduction to form a single phase.
Under standard low-temperature conditions, binary alloys form a single phase only when cooperative reduction occurs.
Five-element systems do not reliably form a single phase when precursor mobility is uncontrolled.
The mechanism primarily applies to noble-metal systems under low-temperature conditions where mobility can be modulated.
The mechanism may not apply in high-temperature, highly diffusive environments or to non-noble-metal systems with different kinetic profiles.
Failure of mobility inhibition to cause a statistically significant and consistent increase in homogeneous single-phase products would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis broadly says that restricted mobility permits homogeneous single-phase formation even with sequential reduction, and the initial state explicitly includes bimetallic mixtures. The predicted outcome and baseline instead say binary systems may, or must, undergo cooperative reduction. The scope of the sequential-reduction claim is therefore inconsistent for binary systems.
